title: Siblings
hookLine: Jacob and Esau, Martha and Mary: sibling love takes work
tomorrow: what's the difference between a friend and a teammate?

cards: A sibling group chat: one sends a photo, another leaves it on read, and an argument about the front seat from age nine is somehow still running. Why do brothers in the Bible fight so much? Cain and Abel.
Joseph sold by his brothers. Jacob and Esau. Even Martha, stuck in the kitchen, asking Jesus to make her sister help.
The Bible doesn't hide it. Sibling love, it seems, takes work.

teach.b: Take the hardest case. Jacob tricks his twin Esau out of their father's blessing and runs for his life. Years later he has to come home, and he's terrified.
He sends gifts ahead and bows low as his brother approaches.
And Genesis says Esau ran to meet him, embraced him, fell on his neck and kissed him, and they wept. Some readers hear that run again in Luke, when the father runs to the son who wasted everything.
The answer here: sibling love isn't the love you're born with. It's the long walk back, and someone willing to run.
Martha's version is smaller and closer to home: Lord, don't you care that my sister has left me to serve alone? Jesus answers her by name, twice, gently, and doesn't take sides in the way she hoped.
Now a neighbor's reading of the same story.
Jews read Jacob and Esau in the Torah, and the commentator Rashi notes that the word kissed has dots written over it in the scroll.
He records two readings. Some say Esau didn't kiss him with his whole heart. Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai says that at that moment Esau's compassion was stirred, and he kissed him with all his heart.
Here's what's shared: both traditions keep this embrace as a picture of brothers coming home. And here's an honest difference. Jewish readers weigh the kiss through the rabbis' debate.
Catholic readers can hear it alongside the Gospel's running father. Two homes for one old story, ranking neither.

how: Catholics read Jacob and Esau in the Old Testament and Martha and Mary in the Gospel at Mass; Jews read Jacob and Esau in the yearly cycle of Torah readings, with commentaries such as Rashi's.

o: the ones who share your table, and the walk back
the oldest child, who speaks for the rest
any two people baptized in the same parish

games.q: brothers and sisters — tap the pairs.

s: Jacob and Esau never made peace
Genesis says Esau ran to meet him, embraced him and kissed him, and they wept.
Rashi records that some readers doubted Esau's kiss
and Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai said his compassion was stirred, and he kissed with all his heart.
Jesus told Mary to get up and help Martha
he answered Martha by name, gently, and didn't take her side the way she hoped.

games.q: you and your brother haven't really talked since a fight over the car. he texts "happy birthday" and nothing else. going by Genesis 33, what's the move?
o: reply "thanks" and wait for a real apology first.
send a long message listing what went wrong.
run toward him: call him back while the door is open.
games.why: Esau didn't wait for a speech; he ran to meet his brother. a small text can be the moment the door opens.

practice: Bring to mind a brother or sister, by birth or by choice, the easy one or the hard one. Open a message to them and type one plain line, the kind that runs toward them a little.
Send it now, later, or not at all; just sit with the line on the screen.

wordCard.voice: Siblings. The ones who share your table and your old fights, and the long walk back. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew, Genesis 33:4: and he kissed him. Rashi notes the dots written over this word.

carryVoice: Pocket this one: brothers and sisters, the kind someone has to run toward. Until tomorrow.
